{{short description|Group of all affine transformations of an affine space}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''affine group''' or '''general affine group''' of any [[affine space]] is the [[group (mathematics)|group]] of all invertible [[affine transformation]]s from the space into itself.  In the case of a [[Euclidean space]] (where the associated field of scalars is the [[real number]]s), the affine group consists of those functions from the space to itself such that the image of every line is a line.

Over any field, the affine group may be viewed as a matrix group in a natural way.  If the associated field of scalars is the real or complex field, then the affine group is a [[Lie group]].

==Relation to general linear group==

===Construction from general linear group===
Concretely, given a vector space {{mvar|V}}, it has an underlying [[affine space]] {{mvar|A}} obtained by "forgetting" the origin, with {{mvar|V}} acting by translations, and the affine group of {{mvar|A}} can be described concretely as the [[semidirect product]] of {{mvar|V}} by {{math|GL(''V'')}}, the [[general linear group]] of {{mvar|V}}:
:<math>\operatorname{Aff}(V) = V \rtimes \operatorname{GL}(V)</math>
The action of {{math|GL(''V'')}} on {{mvar|V}} is the natural one (linear transformations are automorphisms), so this defines a [[semidirect product]].

In terms of matrices, one writes:
:<math>\operatorname{Aff}(n,K) = K^n \rtimes \operatorname{GL}(n,K)</math>
where here the natural action of {{math|GL(''n'', ''K'')}} on {{mvar|K<sup>n</sup>}} is [[matrix multiplication]] of a vector.

===Stabilizer of a point===
Given the affine group of an affine space {{mvar|A}}, the [[Group action (mathematics)#Orbits and stabilizers|stabilizer]] of a point {{mvar|p}} is isomorphic to the general linear group of the same dimension (so the stabilizer of a point in {{math|Aff(2, '''R''')}} is isomorphic to {{math|GL(2, '''R''')}}); formally, it is the general linear group of the vector space {{math|(''A'', ''p'')}}: recall that if one fixes a point, an affine space becomes a [[vector space]].

All these subgroups are conjugate, where conjugation is given by translation from {{mvar|p}} to {{mvar|q}} (which is uniquely defined), however, no particular subgroup is a natural choice, since no point is special – this corresponds to the multiple choices of transverse subgroup, or [[split exact sequence|splitting]] of the [[short exact sequence]]
:<math>1 \to V \to V \rtimes \operatorname{GL}(V) \to \operatorname{GL}(V) \to 1\,.</math>

In the case that the affine group was constructed by ''starting'' with a vector space, the subgroup that stabilizes the origin (of the vector space) is the original {{math|GL(''V'')}}.

==Matrix representation==
Representing the affine group as a semidirect product of {{mvar|V}} by {{math|GL(''V'')}}, then [[Semidirect product#Semidirect products and group homomorphisms|by construction of the semidirect product]], the elements are pairs {{math|(''v'', ''M'')}}, where {{mvar|v}} is a vector in {{mvar|V}} and {{mvar|M}} is a linear transform in {{math|GL(''V'')}}, and multiplication is given by
:<math>(v, M) \cdot (w, N) = (v+Mw, MN)\,.</math>

This can be represented as the {{math|(''n'' + 1) × (''n'' + 1)}} [[block matrix]]
:<math>\left( \begin{array}{c|c} M & v\\ \hline 0 & 1 \end{array}\right) </math>
where {{mvar|M}} is an {{math|''n'' × ''n''}} matrix over {{mvar|K}}, {{mvar|v}} an {{math|''n'' × 1}} column vector, 0 is a {{math|1 × ''n''}} row of zeros, and 1 is the {{nowrap|1 × 1}} identity block matrix.

Formally, {{math|Aff(''V'')}} is naturally isomorphic to a subgroup of {{math|GL(''V'' ⊕ ''K'')}}, with {{mvar|V}} embedded as the affine plane {{math|{(''v'', 1) {{!}} ''v'' ∈ ''V''<nowiki>}</nowiki>}}, namely the stabilizer of this affine plane; the above matrix formulation is the (transpose of the) realization of this, with the {{math|''n'' × ''n''}} and {{math|1 × 1}} blocks corresponding to the direct sum decomposition {{math|''V'' ⊕ ''K''}}.

A [[matrix similarity|similar]] representation is any {{math|(''n'' + 1) × (''n'' + 1)}} matrix in which the entries in each column sum to 1.<ref>{{cite journal|first=David G.|last=Poole|title=The Stochastic Group|journal=[[American Mathematical Monthly]]|volume=102|issue=9|date=November 1995|pages=798–801|doi=10.1080/00029890.1995.12004664 }}</ref> The [[matrix similarity|similarity]] {{mvar|P}} for passing from the above kind to this kind is the {{math|(''n'' + 1) × (''n'' + 1)}} [[identity matrix]] with the bottom row replaced by a row of all ones.

Each of these two classes of matrices is closed under matrix multiplication.

The simplest paradigm may well be the case {{math|''n'' {{=}} 1}}, that is, the upper triangular {{nowrap|2 × 2}} matrices representing the affine group in one dimension. It is a two-parameter [[Non-abelian group|non-Abelian]] [[Lie group]], so with merely two generators (Lie algebra elements), {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}}, such that {{math|[''A'', ''B''] {{=}} ''B''}}, where 
:<math> A= \left( \begin{array}{cc} 1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 \end{array}\right), \qquad B=   \left( \begin{array}{cc} 0 & 1\\ 0 & 0 \end{array}\right)\,,</math>
so that
:<math> e^{aA+bB}= \left( \begin{array}{cc} e^a & \tfrac{b}{a}(e^a-1)\\ 0 & 1 \end{array}\right)\,. </math>

== Character table of {{math|Aff('''F'''{{sub|''p''}})}} ==
{{math|Aff('''F'''{{sub|''p''}})}} has order {{math|''p''(''p'' − 1)}}. Since

:<math>\begin{pmatrix} c & d \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} c & d \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} a & (1-a)d+bc \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\,,</math>

we know {{math|Aff('''F'''{{sub|''p''}})}} has {{mvar|p}} [[conjugacy class]]es, namely

:<math>\begin{align}
C_{id} &= \left\{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\right\}\,, \\[6pt]
C_{1} &= \left\{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & b \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\Bigg|b\in \mathbf{F}_p^*\right\}\,, \\[6pt]
\Bigg\{C_{a} &= \left\{\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\Bigg| b\in \mathbf{F}_p\right\}\Bigg|a\in \mathbf{F}_p\setminus\{0,1\}\Bigg\}\,.
\end{align}</math>

Then we know that {{math|Aff('''F'''{{sub|''p''}})}} has {{mvar|p}} [[irreducible representation]]s. By above paragraph ({{section link|#Matrix representation}}),  there exist {{math|''p'' − 1}} one-dimensional representations, decided by the homomorphism

:<math>\rho_k:\operatorname{Aff}(\mathbf{F}_p)\to\Complex^*</math>

for {{math|''k'' {{=}} 1, 2,… ''p'' − 1}}, where

:<math>\rho_k\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}=\exp\left(\frac{2i kj\pi}{p-1}\right)</math>

and {{math|''i''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} −1}}, {{math|''a'' {{=}} ''g{{isup|j}}''}}, {{mvar|g}} is a generator of the group {{math|'''F'''{{su|b=''p''|p=∗}}}}. Then compare with the order of {{math|'''F'''<sub>''p''</sub>}}, we have

:<math>p(p-1)=p-1+\chi_p^2\,,</math>

hence {{math|''χ<sub>p</sub>'' {{=}} ''p'' − 1}} is the dimension of the last irreducible representation. Finally using the orthogonality of irreducible representations, we can complete the [[character table]] of {{math|Aff('''F'''{{sub|''p''}})}}:

:<math>\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
  &
  {\color{Blue}C_{id}} &
  {\color{Blue}C_1} &
  {\color{Blue}C_g} &
  {\color{Blue}C_{g^2}} &
  {\color{Gray}\dots} &
  {\color{Blue}C_{g^{p-2}}}
\\ \hline
  {\color{Blue}\chi_1} &
  {\color{Gray}1} &
  {\color{Gray}1} &
  {\color{Blue}e^{\frac{2\pi i}{p-1}}} &
  {\color{Blue}e^{\frac{4\pi i}{p-1}}} &
  {\color{Gray}\dots} &
  {\color{Blue}e^{\frac{2\pi (p-2)i}{p-1}}}
\\
  {\color{Blue}\chi_2} &
  {\color{Gray}1} &
  {\color{Gray}1} &
  {\color{Blue}e^{\frac{4\pi i}{p-1}}} &
  {\color{Blue}e^{\frac{8\pi i}{p-1}}} &
  {\color{Gray}\dots} &
  {\color{Blue}e^{\frac{4\pi (p-2)i}{p-1}}}
\\
  {\color{Blue}\chi_3} &
  {\color{Gray}1} &
  {\color{Gray}1} &
  {\color{Blue}e^{\frac{6\pi i}{p-1}}} &
  {\color{Blue}e^{\frac{12\pi i}{p-1}}} &
  {\color{Gray}\dots} &
  {\color{Blue}e^{\frac{6\pi (p-2)i}{p-1}}}
\\
  {\color{Gray}\dots} &
  {\color{Gray}\dots} &
  {\color{Gray}\dots} &
  {\color{Gray}\dots} &
  {\color{Gray}\dots} &
  {\color{Gray}\dots} &
  {\color{Gray}\dots}
\\
  {\color{Blue}\chi_{p-1}} &
  {\color{Gray}1} &
  {\color{Gray}1} &
  {\color{Gray}1} &
  {\color{Gray}1} &
  {\color{Gray}\dots} &
  {\color{Gray}1}
\\
  {\color{Blue}\chi_{p}} &
  {\color{Gray}p-1} &
  {\color{Gray}-1} & 
  {\color{Gray}0} &
  {\color{Gray}0} &
  {\color{Gray}\dots} &
  {\color{Gray}0}
\end{array}</math>

== Planar affine group over the reals==
The elements of <math>\operatorname{Aff}(2,\mathbb R)</math> can take a simple form on a well-chosen [[affine coordinate system]]. More precisely, given an affine transformation of an [[affine plane]] over the [[real number|reals]], an affine coordinate system exists on which it has one of the following forms, where {{mvar|a}}, {{mvar|b}}, and {{mvar|t}} are real numbers (the given conditions insure that transformations are invertible, but not for making the classes distinct; for example, the identity belongs to all the classes).
:<math>\begin{align}
\text{1.}&& (x, y) &\mapsto (x +a,y+b),\\[3pt]
\text{2.}&& (x, y) &\mapsto (ax,by),  &\qquad \text{where } ab\ne 0,\\[3pt]
\text{3.}&& (x, y) &\mapsto (ax,y+b), &\qquad \text{where } a\ne 0,\\[3pt]
\text{4.}&& (x, y) &\mapsto (ax+y,ay), &\qquad \text{where } a\ne 0,\\[3pt]
\text{5.}&& (x, y) &\mapsto (x+y,y+a)\\[3pt]
\text{6.}&& (x, y) &\mapsto (a(x\cos t + y\sin t), a(-x\sin t+y\cos t)), &\qquad \text{where } a\ne 0.
\end{align}</math>

Case 1 corresponds to [[Translation (geometry)|translation]]s.

Case 2 corresponds to [[scaling (geometry)|scalings]] that may differ in two different directions. When working with a [[Euclidean plane]] these directions need not be [[perpendicular]], since the [[coordinate axes]] need not be perpendicular.

Case 3 corresponds to a scaling in one direction and a translation in another one.

Case 4 corresponds to a [[shear mapping]] combined with a dilation.

Case 5 corresponds to a [[shear mapping]] combined with a dilation.

Case 6 corresponds to [[similarity (geometry)|similarities]] when the coordinate axes are perpendicular.

The affine transformations without any [[fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]] belong to cases 1, 3, and 5. The transformations that do not preserve the orientation of the plane belong to cases 2 (with {{math|''ab'' < 0}}) or 3 (with {{math|''a'' < 0}}).

The proof may be done by first remarking that if an affine transformation has no fixed point, then the matrix of the associated linear map has an [[eigenvalue]] equal to one, and then using the [[Jordan normal form#Real matrices|Jordan normal form theorem for real matrices]].

==Other affine groups and subgroups==

===General case===
Given any subgroup {{math|''G'' < GL(''V'')}} of the [[general linear group]], one can produce an affine group, sometimes denoted {{math|Aff(''G'')}}, analogously as {{math|Aff(''G'') :{{=}} ''V'' ⋊ ''G''}}.

More generally and abstractly, given any group {{mvar|G}} and a [[group representation|representation]] <math>\rho : G \to \operatorname{GL}(V)</math> of {{mvar|G}} on a vector space {{mvar|V}}, one gets<ref group="note">Since {{math|GL(''V'') < Aut(''V'')}}. Note that this containment is in general proper, since by "automorphisms" one means ''group'' automorphisms, i.e., they preserve the group structure on {{mvar|V}} (the addition and origin), but not necessarily scalar multiplication, and these groups differ if working over {{math|'''R'''}}.</ref> an associated affine group {{math|''V'' ⋊<sub>''ρ''</sub> ''G''}}: one can say that the affine group obtained is "a [[group extension]] by a vector representation", and, as above, one has the short exact sequence
<math display="block">1 \to V \to V \rtimes_\rho G \to G \to 1.</math>

===Special affine group===
The subset of all invertible affine transformations that preserve a fixed [[volume form]] up to sign is called the ''special affine group''.  (The transformations themselves are sometimes called ''equiaffinities''.)  This group is the affine analogue of the [[special linear group]].  In terms of the semi-direct product, the special affine group consists of all pairs {{math|(''M'', ''v'')}} with <math>|\det(M)| = 1</math>, that is, the affine transformations
<math display="block">x \mapsto Mx + v</math>
where {{mvar|M}} is a linear transformation of whose determinant has absolute value 1 and {{mvar|v}} is any fixed translation vector.<ref>{{cite book|first=M.|last=Berger|author-link=Marcel Berger|date=1987|title=Geometry|volume=1|at=Section 2.7.6|location=Berlin Heidelberg|publisher=Springer-Verlag|isbn=9780534000349}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|first=Günter|last=Ewald|date=1971|title=Geometry: An Introduction|at=Section 4.12|location=Belmont|publisher=Wadsworth|isbn=9780534000349}}</ref>

The subgroup of the special affine group consisting of those transformations whose linear part has determinant 1 is the group of orientation- and volume-preserving maps.  Algebraically, this group is a semidirect product <math>SL(V) \ltimes V</math> of the special linear group of <math>V</math> with the translations.  It is generated by the [[shear mapping]]s.<!--<ref>todo</ref>-->

===Projective subgroup===
Presuming knowledge of [[projectivity]] and the projective group of [[projective geometry]], the affine group can be easily specified. For example, Günter Ewald wrote:<ref>{{cite book|first=Günter|last=Ewald|date=1971|title=Geometry: An Introduction|page=241|location=Belmont|publisher=Wadsworth|isbn=9780534000349}}</ref>
:The set <math>\mathfrak{P}</math> of all projective collineations of {{math|''P''{{isup|''n''}}}} is a group which we may call the '''projective group''' of {{math|''P''{{isup|''n''}}}}. If we proceed from {{math|''P''{{isup|''n''}}}} to the affine space {{math|''A''{{isup|''n''}}}} by declaring a [[hyperplane]] {{mvar|ω}} to be a [[hyperplane at infinity]], we obtain the '''affine group''' <math>\mathfrak{A}</math> of {{math|''A''{{isup|''n''}}}} as the [[subgroup]] of <math>\mathfrak{P}</math> consisting of all elements of <math>\mathfrak{P}</math> that leave {{mvar|ω}} fixed.
::<math>\mathfrak{A} \subset \mathfrak{P}</math>

===Isometries of Euclidean space===
{{main|Euclidean group}}
When the affine space {{mvar|A}} is a Euclidean space (over the field of real numbers), the group <math>\mathcal{E}</math> of distance-preserving maps (''[[isometry|isometries]]'') of {{mvar|A}} is a subgroup of the affine group.  Algebraically, this group is a semidirect product <math>O(V) \ltimes V</math> of the [[orthogonal group]] of <math>V</math> with the translations.  Geometrically, it is the subgroup of the affine group generated by the orthogonal reflections.<!--<ref>Todo</ref>-->

===Poincaré group===
{{main|Poincaré group}}
The [[Poincaré group]] is the affine group of the [[Lorentz group]] {{math|O(1,3)}}:
:<math>\mathbf{R}^{1,3}\rtimes \operatorname{O}(1,3)</math>

This example is very important in [[Theory of relativity|relativity]].
